description:
The most commonly asked question in English is probably “How are you?” In this video, we’ll provide you with a variety of answers that go beyond the common ones! 
-------
FAQ's:

Can you use these answers for everyone?
It depends! Saying something like "I’m having a good day, how about yourself?" is perfect for your boss or teacher, but too casual for a close friend. We go over 20 different answers to "How are you", ranging from unique and casual to polite and formal.

Do native speakers actually use all of these phrases?
Native English speakers use many of these phrases, but not ALL of them! Some of these answers are unique, while others are common in everyday life.

What should I say if I'm having a bad day?
It depends who you're talking to. You could tell just about anyone, "I’ve had better days," and it would still be polite enough to use for a coworker.

title: Ranking English Teaching Methods from 1 to 10 | Language Teaching Methods & Approaches with Jackie
description:
In this video, Jackie ranks the most popular English-teaching methods from 1 to 10.  This video goes over 10 different English teaching methods from Communicative Language Teaching (CLT), to Test-Teach-Test (TTT), and which teaching method works for what students.

Continue watching to find out where YOUR preferred teaching methods rank.

--------------------------------------------------------
Transcript:
I'm going to rate language teaching methods. 10 is an excellent method and one is a method that I don't like and would probably never use. All right, let's get to it. 

Communicative language teaching. CLT is all the rage today. I'm going to give it a 10. If you're serious about students actually being able to communicate in English, this is kind of where it's at. 

The grammar translation approach, I would give it a five. If your students want to learn how to translate from one language into English, it's great. All other motivations, it's not great. 

Total physical response, I'd give it a seven for kids. Adults, I'd give it maybe a three. It's quite fun for students to say like stand up, touch your head, that kind of thing, but it's a bit of a it's a bit babyish for adults. 

Audio lingual method. The audioingual method is focused on building habits. This is what most of the language learning apps are based on. I would give it maybe a six or seven. It's probably better for self-study than it is for teachers to be using in class. 

The direct method. The direct method uses only English in class. I would give this maybe a one or a two for total beginners, but if you're teaching kind of high beginners or intermediate or advanced, I would give it a eight or nine or a 10. 

The natural approach. So the natural approach is when you teach a language starting with like first listening and then you kind of get into speaking and then you get into reading and writing later. It's like how babies learn a language. They first listen and then they start talking using simple sentences and they get into more complicated sentences. I would give this maybe a six. It's not a bad way to learn or teach English, but there's often a lot of benefit to teaching students how to read first because they can learn vocabulary and do kind of self-study on their own. 

Task based teaching, I would give task-based teaching a nine or a 10. Of course, it depends on the teacher and how well you choose and set up the task based on the age and the level of the students. 

The lexical approach. So, the lexical approach f focuses on chunks of language. So, example, collocations or idioms like fast food, it's raining cats and dogs, something like that. I love the lexical approach, and I would give it maybe a nine or 10 because it can help students to speak more fluently. 

Content and language integrated learning (CLIL). So this is where a teacher would maybe teach, for example, an introduction to economics in English. I would give this a seven or an eight. It really depends on the students. If the students are high enough level to kind of grasp the concepts and ideas they need to learn about economics, it pushes it up to a 10. 

Test, teach, test. So the test, teach, test approach is ideal. If you think that students have studied something many times before, so for example, the simple past. So I would give students a quick test, find out what they know and what they don't know. Then I would teach I would tailor the lesson to what they don't know. Then I would give a little simple test again to find out if students have learned what I was trying to teach them. I would give this method a 10 for anyone who is not a total beginner. It's such a good method to find out.

Transcript:
Today I'm going to talk about what is content and language integrated learning. Calil, C L I L for short. 

This is when you learn a foreign or a second language in an academic context with academic content. This could often be see in universities in Europe or in South Korea, where maybe someone, a native English speaker would teach introduction to psychology or introduction to economics in English to Korean students or to Swedish students or whoever. 

The CLIl method involves the four C's. There's content, communication, cognition and culture. 

Some of the benefits of CLIL are that it's an immersive environment. It can help students increase fluency in that subject matter in English. It focuses on authentic contexts, not ones that are just common in ESL textbooks. By the time students say get to like university in South Korea, they're probably quite tired of talking about the weather, sports, hobbies, etc. in English. Using this method and teaching about say psychology or economics or whatever is often more interesting for students than kind of the standard old topics that are often covered way too often in most textbooks. 

The biggest negative to content and language integrated learning is that if students are not proficient in English, they may not grasp the content that's being taught. For example, say I was in Korea at a Korean university, and I was teaching an introduction to psychology to psychology majors. If a student wasn't that good at English, they may not grasp the concepts that they need to be learning about psychology as a foundation for the rest of their studies. So that's the major thing. 

If students are quite good at English, that's not a problem. But the weaker students really may struggle to grasp the key concepts about that subject matter that you want them to learn. Okay, so that's basically it for CLIL. title: The Audio-Lingual Method: What Is It & Is It Effective? | English Teaching Tips with Jackie
description:
What is the audio-lingual method, and is it effective for teaching English? In this video, I go over the audio-lingual method, what it consists of, where it thrives, and if it's an effective method for teaching English to students.

Continue watching to find out more...
-------
FAQ's for this video:

Which teaching method is best for absolute beginners?
Teachers frequently search for methods that lower the affective filter and build foundational confidence. Many researchers and practitioners suggest a blend, often pointing to the Audio-Lingual Method for basic structural habit-building or Total Physical Response for kinesthetic learning in early stages.

How do I adapt traditional methods for large, mixed-ability classes?
Managing a diverse classroom is a constant challenge. Teachers look for ways to scale methods like Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) so that students at different proficiency levels can still engage meaningfully without the teacher needing to provide constant, individual feedback to every student.

How do I balance grammatical accuracy with fluency?
This is perhaps the most persistent debate in ESL. Educators look for frameworks on when to correct errors and when to prioritize the flow of communication. The search often leads to discussions on whether explicit grammar instruction (common in older methods) or communicative practice (common in newer methods) serves the student better in the long run.

Is the audiolingual method effective for teaching language? 

First of all, what is the audiolingual method? It focuses mostly on drills. Kind of repeat after me. Changing one word, focusing on patterns. The main focus of this method is building habits, grammatical accuracy, and pronunciation. It can be effective if your goal is to improve your pronunciation or to speak fluently and quickly. It can increase confidence in the target structures and it can be good for large classes where the teacher may not be able to give personal feedback to all of the students. 

However, the audiolingual method is actually not that effective for real world communication because people don't speak in like these very precise grammatical structures with only a very precise certain set of vocabulary. People use a lot of grammatical structures and a lot of different vocabulary, and this method is just kind of too narrow to really take that into account and there's really no focus on skills besides speaking. 

So I would say it can be good in certain situations, maybe for absolute beginners when you have a very large class. It can be effective for certain things. However, it's better as part of a larger program.

Here are the best methods for teaching language to high school students. So, high school students can be a little bit tricky because they're not children. So, you don't want to teach obviously topics for children like colors or numbers and stuff like that, but they're also not adults. So, it can be difficult to talk about, you know, more adult things like banking or buying a house or stuff like that. So, you have to kind of, there's a middle ground um with high school students. 

So here are some of the things that I like to do with them in my own classes. The first one is task based learning. So this is where students have to complete a task of some kind and they can kind of go at their own pace and focus on what they want to learn. So some good examples of tasks that I might use with high school students are to plan a class party or to plan a trip on the summer vacation. They could do that alone or generally I like to do that kind of activity in groups and then they can do um a little presentation in front of the class. 

The second idea I have for high school students is debate. So choose some controversial topics and then get students talking about it, sharing opinions and ideas and supporting those reasons with evidence and facts. I also like to use songs and podcasts and movies and TV show clips in my classes with high school students. So, I won't like watch an entire movie in a class. I find that quite difficult and most students will end up sleeping by the end of that class, but if you show little clips or maybe like a 5 or 10 minute podcast. I like to give students questions that they have to answer and then it can lead into some nice discussion after that. 

Something else that high school students really enjoy is learning about slang and idioms in English. So, chances are almost no textbooks have the up-to-date slang that people are using, but if you can do a lesson on that, it can be quite fun for students. 

Another thing I like to do in my classes with teenagers and also adults is board games. You can make up your own board games um kind of just based on whatever you're teaching students. Some things that work well are like the simple past or like should or shouldn't. And you can make a little grid and then make some little questions and stuff like that on your on your paper. or if students are a little bit higher level, I like to bring real board games into my class. For example, Settlers of Catan or King of Tokyo or something like that.

Games in general. So, even though high school students seem like maybe mini adults in some ways in the fact that they can kind of sit still for a while and maybe do some more serious kind of like reading lessons or something like that, I like to mix up a game into my lessons almost every class. So, we might do some more serious stuff at the beginning, but then I like to end with a game to kind of reinforce what I've been teaching that class. 

And the final idea I have for teaching language to high school students is to use a lesson plan. Always use a lesson plan. If you fail to plan, you plan to fail. So I like to start with kind of like setting the context, which a little icebreaker or an introduction to whatever I'm teaching. Then maybe introduce some language and then have some controlled practice and then some freer practice and then maybe ending off with a game. So, that is like a very general overview of how I would plan a language lesson for any age or level.

The third roleplay idea is ordering food. So students can one person can be the waiter or waitress or the fast food employee and the other student can order whatever they would like.

USA versus UK English. Mail versus post. If you write a letter to your grandma or a card, you could say in the USA, I'm going to mail the letter. However, in the UK, you could say, I'm going to post this letter. 

Holiday versus vacation. In the US, you would say, I'm going to take a vacation, which is a break from work. But in the UK, you would say, "I'm going to go on holiday or I'm going to take holidays," which is a break from work. 

Dessert versus pudding. So, if you want a little something sweet after your meal, maybe a little cake or like some fruit or something, in the USA, you would call that dessert, but in the UK, you would say pudding. 

Oatmeal versus porridge. Oatmeal is what something you would eat for breakfast in the USA. In the UK, it's the same, but you would call it porridge. So it's kind of like a hot cereal mix. 

Aubergine versus eggplant. In the US, that long purple vegetable, you would call it an eggplant. However, in the UK, you would call it an oberine. 

Sneakers versus trainers. So kind of the athletic shoes that you would wear when you play sports. In the USA, you would call them sneakers. However, in the UK, you would call them trainers.

Transcript:
Hi, this is Jackie from eslactivity.org. Here are my top tips for teaching pronunciation to English learners. The first thing is to teach students minimal pairs. So, minimal pairs are words that vary just by one letter sound. Example, bat and bet. The only difference is the vowel, the a or the e, or pip or pit. The only difference is the end of this word with P or T. So teaching students these minimal pairs can really be helpful at differentiating the small sounds in English. 

The second thing I like to do with my students is repeat after me. I know that sometimes teachers feel a little bit shy about it. I often feel shy getting students to repeat after me, but it actually can be a very helpful thing. Particularly if you're a native speaker, your pronunciation is probably perfect. So getting students to repeat after you can be a helpful exercise. 

The next tip I have for teaching pronunciation is to focus on the shape of your mouth and get students to focus on the shapes of their mouths. For example, pip and pit. You notice with pip your mouth is closed. Pit your mouth is open. So there's rules and kind of different mouth shapes for the various letter sounds in English. So get if students are struggling with pronunciation. For example, the difference between a P and a T. The shape of the mouth is often the key factor. Another thing that can really help students with pronunciation is focusing on the vowel sounds in English. There's a whole bunch of rules for the double ones. Teaching students the rules explicitly can really help them with pronunciation. 

The next tip I have for teaching pronunciation is to focus on chunks and connected speech. So, for example, nobody would really say, "I want to go to the store tonight." Instead, you'd probably say, "I want to go to the store tonight." You wouldn't write out wanna to when you're writing. You would write, "I want to." But when you're speaking, you would put it all together. I want to go to the store tonight. Focusing on things like this can really help students to sound more natural. 

Another tip I have for teaching pronunciation is to teach contractions. Nobody would really say, "I would like to get some ice cream." You would maybe write it, "I would like to get some ice cream." But when you're speaking, you'd say, "I'd like to get some ice cream." When you speak, you almost always use contractions. Make sure to point out to students the difference between writing and spoken English in terms of contractions. 

All right, the last tip I have is to focus on stress and intonation, particularly on the multi-syllable words. So sometimes my experience when I was teaching in Korea is the students would be trying to say a long word and I genuinely would have no idea what they were saying. I just was like, "What? I'm not I I don't understand what you're saying." And then I would say sometimes like, "Write it out. Just spell it out for me." And they would write it on their paper. And I'd say, "Oh, you mean beautiful." Or it's like was quite a simple word, but it was not really understandable because their pronunciation or their stress or their in intonation was incorrect. So point out in words and sentences where the stress should lie. 

Those are my top tips for teaching pronunciation to English learners. If you like these activities or these ideas, please be sure to check out my book, 101 ESL Activities for Teenagers and Adults.

How can I remember grammar rules when I'm actually speaking?
Many students understand grammar in a textbook but can freeze during a conversation. Focus on practicing conversations with English speakers at first, rather than just grammar rules.

Is it better to learn slang or proper English first?
It depends on the situation! Learning slang first can make it seem more natural, but English slang varies from region to region, and learning formal English first is best.

Hi, this is Jackie from eslleactivity.org. So, if you're interested in teaching English in a foreign country, I'm going to talk about the basic requirements that you need. First of all, I want to say that it really varies by country. Some places require you to have a certain passport, say from Canada or the US or England, have a BA, while others maybe just require a TESL certificate, maybe you can volunteer, etc. So, whatever country you're looking to teach in, be sure to check the requirements closely because it really, really can vary. 

So, the first thing that you'll need is a passport. If you want to travel outside your country, of course, this is something you need. However, a passport from the big six countries can really go a lot further. So, the big six in the English teaching world are Canada, USA, England, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa. So, those are countries where English is spoken as the first language. If you want to teach in a place like South Korea, you'll need to have a passport from one of these countries, and there's kind of no way around that.

 The second requirement is a BA degree. So, generally, a 4-year degree, although some three-year degrees may be accepted in some places. This isn't a strict requirement as there are a few countries, especially in like South America, that may not require this, but generally you'll need a 4-year degree from an English-speaking university. 

The next thing you might need is a TEFL or a CELTA certificate. So, generally, this is a 120-hour certificate of some kind. Not all countries require this, but some do. And the countries that even may maybe might not require it. If you have it, you can often get kind of bumped up on the pay scale or get a little bit higher pay. 

The next thing you need for teaching English abroad is some cash. I know that sounds kind of strange to say you're going to go work and do a job in another country. So, why would you need to bring cash with you if you're going to get paid there? However, the way things work out, you might not actually be paid until a month or 6 weeks after you start teaching. So, you'll need some money to kind of get up and running and buy a few things for your apartment, etc. Generally, I recommend a minimum of $1 to $2,000. That's kind of at the lower end. FAQ's in this video:
What is the primary focus of competency-based language teaching?
This approach focuses on practical, real-life tasks that learners need to navigate their daily lives, such as ordering food on the phone or filling out job applications, rather than learning random grammar and vocabulary that may not be immediately applicable 

How is student progress assessed in this method?

What are the four core competency areas?

It was developed in the 1970s as kind of a survival method for newcomers or refugees to an English-speaking country where they just had to survive and kind of know the basics, just enough to communicate in whatever situation or context that they found themselves in. 

This method focuses on what learners do in real life. They're not just learning kind of random grammar and vocabulary that might be applicable at some point in the future. Maybe or maybe not. They're learning things that they need for today or tomorrow to go to the store, to order some food on the phone, to talk to the maybe the postman or postwoman, something like that. 

For this method, assessment is not made in comparison to other students as would be like in a traditional language learning class. It's made against benchmarks. So, for example, can a student order food on the phone? Yes or no? Or can a student maybe fill out a job application form? Yes or no. So, students are kind of measured against themselves and what tasks they can complete that are relevant for their daily life. 

This method has four competency areas. The first one is interacting with others. The second one is understanding instructions. The third one is getting things done. And the fourth one is sharing information that you need.

So, today's idiom is beat me to the punch. Beat me to the punch. It means someone did something before you. It comes from boxing. If the two people are fighting, if this person can do the first punch and it's a knockout punch, he will be the winner. And this guy didn't even throw one punch because he beat him to the punch. So, here's an example. You have two companies, and this company came out with some amazing innovation, some new product and this company was develing developing it, but they were too slow. So they'd say, "Oh, they beat us to the punch." Or if you want to buy something on sale, there's only one left. You were fighting. You got it. You can say, "I beat her to the punch." It means you got it first. You did it first. 

So today's idiom is a tough nut to crack or a hard nut to crack. Tough and hard are very similar. So, a tough nut to crack is someone who is difficult to get to know. It comes from, if you think about nuts, like a walnut for example, you can't really break a walnut with your bare hands. You need a special tool of some kind. So that's why it's called a hard nut to crack. All right, some examples. My boss is a tough nut to crack. I'm not even sure if he likes me. Next one. My husband is a hard nut to crack. It took me years to get to know him when we were dating. And finally, I've heard that Professor Bolan is a tough nut to crack. It's difficult to get an A in her class. 

So today's idiom is barking up the wrong tree. This comes from hunting. When hunting dogs were used, the dogs would run around looking for animals in trees, and they would bark at the bottom of the tree so their owners could shoot the animal, the bird or the raccoon or whatever was in the tree. But sometimes the dogs were wrong. They were barking at a tree, but there were actually no animals in that tree. So what this means is you blame someone for something, but it's not their fault. For example, two children and maybe something is broken, and the dad says, "Hey, you broke that thing." And this kid says, "You're barking up the wrong tree. It was my brother." So, you're blaming him, but he didn't do it. It was actually his brother. So, his dad is barking up the wrong tree.

Today I'm going to talk about the lexical approach to teaching languages. What is the lexical approach? It focuses on lexical units or word chunks, not necessarily grammatical structures. 

The lexical approach focuses on collocations and chunks. Some examples of collocations are bad hair day, rescue attempt, fast food. These are words that occur together more commonly than by random chance. Fast food is often seen together. 

Chunks are words that are phrases that are often found together. For example, how are you? Thanks for helping me, something like that. 

The lexical approach generally uses authentic materials, those found in real life, not necessarily designed for English learners. Students notice the chunks or the collocations rather than focusing on grammar or being explicitly told to memorize a certain phrase. 

The goal of the lexical approach is to be more natural-sounding and to focus on fluency. That's basically it for the lexical approach, just an overview. It focuses on phrases, chunks, collocations, etc., rather than focusing explicitly on grammatical rules.

What does slay mean? Slay means kill it or to do an exceptionally good job of something. For example, she slayed that presentation. Your outfit is slaying. 

What is quiet quitting? Quiet quitting is when you do the absolute bare minimum at a job. So, you follow the job description exactly and you don't do anything extra. It's when you show up at exactly 9:00, you take your full 1 hour lunch break from 12 to 1, and then you leave at exactly 4:00 or 5:00 whenever you're finished for the day. It's basically not doing anything beyond the absolute bare minimum in order to not get fired. 

What is chewy? Chewy describes something that's outdated, uncool, or trying too hard to be cool but not succeeding. I hope you don't feel like that about me. Anyway, here are some examples. Wearing skinny jeans is so chewy. My dad's obsession with that rapper is very chewy. 

What does it mean to be a stan of something or someone? This comes from Eminem's song with the same name, Stan, where there's a fan who is obsessed with him. Here are some examples. I stan Taylor Swift so hard. I used to stan Beyonce when I was younger, but not so much these days. I love Conor McDavid. I've been a Stan since the Oilers drafted him. 

What's Riz? Riz means style, charm, or attractiveness related to a romantic partner. For example, he has great riz. My date last night had so much riz, I'm totally into him. Riz is basically short for charisma. 

When someone says you ate something, but it's not related to food, what does that mean? It means you express approval or admiration about someone's achievement. For example, you ate that outfit. You ate that dance routine. She ate that presentation. 

What does it mean to be caught in 4K? It means you've been caught doing something wrong on camera. The footage is such high quality that it's undeniable that it's you. For example, he tried to sneak out last night, but I caught him in 4K. She was caught cheating in 4K. What a scandal. That politician was caught in 4K saying contradictory things. 

What does he gave me the ick or she gave me the ick mean? It means in a romantic relationship someone did something that just kind of grossed you out, such that you're no longer attracted to them. It could be really anything that turns you off about someone. It doesn't have to be like they smell bad. It could just be like maybe even something simple, the way they eat, or just they walk kind of strangely, or they wore like a weird sweater or something like that. It's anything that just kind of makes you say no. Or it can be something that kind of just makes you feel a little bit uncomfortable, even if you can't really put your finger on it. 

What does it mean to be ratioed? This is when you do a social media post, quite often on Twitter where you get more negative attention and comments than you do positive ones. Here are some examples. Oh, we just got ratioed. That new campaign got ratioed. So, this basically means that most people disagree with what you said, or you said something very controversial while people where people have very strong opinions.

FAQ's on English slang:
"Is it appropriate for me to use this slang?"
You want to make sure you know if a term is professional enough for a work environment, if it might be considered rude or offensive, or if it is only suitable for specific social groups (like friends or peers) before using specific slang.

Why doesn't this phrase make sense literally?
Many slang expressions are figurative, and translating them word-for-word often leads to confusion. It's meant to be a fun turn of phrase.

How do I keep up with slang that changes so quickly?
Since slang trends evolve rapidly due to social media and pop culture, English learners often feel overwhelmed by trying to stay current. You can frequently ask for advice on how to find up-to-date resources, how to tell if a word is already outdated or "cringey," and how to distinguish between permanent vocabulary and temporary internet trends.

Transcript:
Here's an educational time filler. Just a minute. So, this is kind of a Toastmaster style activity. 

I put students in groups of four, and I write a bunch of words on the board, and they relate to things that students could talk about for one minute quite easily. So, for example, food, hobbies, TV shows, um after school, etc. Then the students give themselves a number in their group, 1 2 3 4. 

And then one student will throw a little paper scrunched up paper ball at the board. Whatever word it hits, the first person in each group has to talk about that for one minute without stopping. The other three people in the group have to listen and then ask a follow-up question at the end of that minute. 

And then when that's done, throw another piece of paper at the board and the second topic and the second student will go until all four students have done the activity.

description:

Timestamp for ESL games video: 
0:00 Intro
0:10 What is a comparative anda superlative adjective?
0:29 1st idea: Putting students in pairs
0:40 2nd idea: Hot potato
1:10 3rd idea: Picture prompt
1:25 4th idea: Dialogue substitution
2:04 5th idea: Boardgames
2:44 6th idea: Conversation starter
3:03 7th idea: Disappearing text
3:36 Final thoughts

Transcript:
Today I'm going to talk about my favorite comparative and superlative adjective activities. What is a comparative adjective? It's when you compare two things. For example, that building is taller than this building or that person is shorter than this person. A superlative means like the most of something. That's the biggest or tallest building in the city or she's the shortest person in the class. 

My first simple idea for an activity is to put students into pairs, and they have to make some sentences. I'm older than him, or he's taller than me. 

The second idea I have is to play hot potato. So you can get some music on YouTube. There's even like hot potato music that stops automatically. Students can pass around an object. I like to do a soft object just for safety in the classroom. Maybe like a little stuffed animal or something. When the music stops, I show students two flash cards. Maybe there's a pig and a dog, and students have to make a sentence with those two things using a comparative adjective. For example, pigs are usually bigger than dogs. 

The third idea I have is to use picture prompt. You can put a big picture up on the screen and then students can make some sentences using what they see. For example, the woman looks older than the man or the child is shorter than his mom. 

The next idea I have is dialogue substitution. If you're using a textbook, there's probably a dialogue that has comparative adjectives or superlative adjectives in it. If you ask students to read it together in pairs, they kind of just blow through it without really paying attention to what they read. And it's not really the students fault. It's because I haven't really given them a reason to actually pay attention to what they're reading. Instead, I like to remove the comparative and superlative adjectives, put them in a little word bank at the top, and then students have to read it carefully and fill in the blanks. 

The next idea I have is board games. It's very easy to just make your own. So using a grid, maybe 5x5 on Google documents or whatever and then I put some fun squares move two spaces ahead, trade spaces with the person on your left, etc. In the other ones I would put some words. For example tall, short, best, good, worst, etc. When students land on that square, so for example maybe they land on best, they have to make a sentence. For example, the best teacher is Jackie. And if they can make a correct sentence that kind of fits and makes sense, they stay on that space. If they don't, they have to go back to where they started. 

The next idea I have is a conversation starter. I give students some conversation starters related to this topic. For example, it's been the worst day and the students have to continue that conversation, maybe talking about why, or I had the best weekend, and then students can continue that conversation. 

The final idea I have is disappearing text. So this is kind of just a nice review at the end of class if you have a minute or two. So you can write a sentence on the board. For example, the best movie is Forest Gump. And I can get students to say the whole sentence out loud, and then I can erase a few words, and students can still say that sentence. Then I erase a couple more words or the whole sentence, and they can say that out loud. 

Okay, so those are my top activities for comparative and superlative adjectives. If you like these activities, please hit like, subscribe, and be sure to check out my book 101 ESL Activities for Teenagers and Adults.

title: Chief Paulino Retirement
description:
Congratulations to Chief of District Police Joseph Paulino, on your retirement.

On July 1, 2010, Chief Joseph Paulino was sworn in as Chief of Police for the San Bernardino City Unified School District Police Department.
On October 1, 1997, he was hired as a “lateral” police officer from the Los Angeles County Safety Police Department.  He is a graduate of Rio Hondo Police Academy.    
Prior to his law enforcement assignments, he served in the Army for 10 years; his last three years as a Sergeant in the 10th Mountain Division, 1-87 Infantry. 
Chief Paulino is currently in the process of working on his Doctoral Degree at Liberty University. He has earned a Master’s Degree in Public Administration and a Bachelor of Science in Workforce Education from Southern Illinois University at Carbondale. In June, 1998, he earned an Associate of Arts Degree in Administration of Justice at San Bernardino Valley College, San Bernardino, CA.
His extensive law enforcement leadership training includes graduation from the prestigious FBI National Academy, POST’s Role of the Chief Course and Executive Development Course. In addition, he has been awarded the POST Basic, Intermediate, Advance, Management and Executive Certificates.   
During his tenure with the department, Chief Paulino has served as an Assistant Director, Lieutenant, Watch Commander, Patrol Sergeant and Patrol Officer.  
In 1999, he was selected by his peers and the San Bernardino Area Chamber of Commerce as “Officer of the Year” and in 2013 received the National We Tip Award of “Chief of the Year”. He has also served as the Chair for the Safety Training Association Representing San Bernardino County (STARS).  He is an active member of the following organizations: Kappa Alpha Psi, Thinkwise Credit Union Executive Board, NOBLE, San Bernardino Chaplains Board, FBI-NAA, FBILEEDA, WeTip National Executive Board, International Footprint-Chapter 67, American Legion-Post 14, Kiwanis and San Bernardino Countywide Gang and Drug Taskforce Executive Board. 
He and his wife, Elsie, reside in Colton and have three children - Jay, Joey and Zana.
